A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ORIC research work. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison, including tracking material relocated in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, sampling ablations, object-size and prompting analyses, and a manual audit of 300 generated questions.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark evaluations and adds Visual-RFT experiments, evaluation against human-provided labels, and results on AMBER and HallusionBench.

M1.justification: v1 proposes benchmark construction through LLM- and CLIP-guided sampling. v2 additionally adapts Visual-RFT to train Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct using GRPO, correctness and format rewards, and structured reasoning outputs. It also reports switching the positive-question selection model from GPT-4o to GPT-5.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluations on HallusionBench, covering visual illusions and abstract figures, and AMBER, covering existence, attributes, and relations. These benchmarks were discussed but not experimentally evaluated in v1. COCO-based contextual recognition and POPE comparisons remain.

E2.justification: The full comparisons replace GPT-4o with GPT-5 and Qwen2.5-VL-7B with Qwen3-VL-8B. Table 1 replaces LLaVA with Qwen3; the sampling ablation and object-size comparison replace Janus-Pro with Qwen3. The new fine-tuning study includes untuned Qwen3 with and without zero-shot CoT as controls. Other models omitted from the shortened main table remain in the appendix.

E3.justification: v2 introduces full-parameter training on 600 balanced questions from COCO-2014 training images, disjoint from benchmark validation images, for 15 epochs with eight rollouts per group. It also introduces a separate 200-question evaluation using human-provided ground truth. For existing evaluations, the reported fallback answer matcher changes from GPT-4o to GPT-5; four-prompt averaging, the token limit, and detector threshold remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds checks of fine-tuning performance against alternative human labels and generalization across visual and semantic benchmark conditions. v1's four-model zero-shot CoT analysis is removed and replaced by Qwen3-focused CoT and fine-tuning comparisons. Sampling ablations, object-size analyses, image-similarity analysis, and the original annotation-error cases remain, with some moved to appendices.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals for the same CLIPScore analysis and average benchmark results over four prompts. v2 adds no seed counts, repeated-training estimates, significance tests, or uncertainty intervals for its new fine-tuning results.

E6.justification: v2 adds GPT-5 and Qwen3 results and reports Qwen3 macro F1 increasing from 79.55 to 82.79 after Visual-RFT, with human-label F1 increasing from 78.63 to 83.62. Figure 5 adds HallusionBench results of 69.37 versus 69.81 and AMBER results of 87.48 versus 90.49 for untuned versus fine-tuned Qwen3. Table 1 also changes InternVL3's POPE-subset F1 from 100.0 to 95.99. These include new model comparisons, not same-model improvements across PDF versions.

T1.justification: v2 adds a probabilistic formulation involving object-context distributions and assumptions about conflicting ROI evidence and contextual priors in Section 2.1. Section 5 introduces formal reward normalization, token advantages, likelihood ratios, and the GRPO optimization objective. These extend v1's construction, similarity, and metric definitions; no new theorem or proof is provided.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from a diagnostic benchmark to a framework generating both evaluation and training data. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly claim that contextual incongruity creates uncertainty and that ORIC-based reinforcement fine-tuning mitigates errors, transfers across benchmarks, and improves alignment with human reasoning.

C2.justification: v2 adds an uncertainty-based mechanism involving weak local evidence, strong contextual priors, and binary supervision encouraging guesses. It interprets fine-tuning gains as better evidence-grounded reasoning and agreement with human reasoning, although the reported human comparison measures answer-label agreement. The COCO-source limitation and discussion of CLIPScore's limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds a substantial training specification: AdamW, learning rate 2e-6, clipping, batching, rollout settings, BF16, zero KL penalty, four H100 GPUs, and an R1-style prompt. Figure 6 also changes the sampling prompt from relying on contextual priors to explicitly avoiding them, creating ambiguity relative to the retained method description. The code-access URL is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 connects ORIC to a newly cited account of why language models hallucinate and adds a dedicated reinforcement-learning discussion covering Visual-RFT, DeepSeek-R1, GRPO-related work, o1, and RLHF-V. This substantially broadens the positioning from recognition benchmarking to uncertainty-oriented model improvement.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contextual-incongruity discussion, and results narrative are extensively rewritten around uncertainty and mitigation. Evaluation material is reorganized, several analyses move into appendices, and separate mitigation-method and experiment sections are introduced. Terminology distinguishes the ORIC framework from ORIC-Bench, and the title and author block change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the opening examples, transposes Table 2 and removes its LLM-free-evaluation category, and splits the full main results into a shorter main table and an appendix table. It adds fine-tuning and training-configuration tables and a training-prompt figure, replaces the old CoT chart with cross-benchmark results, and relocates several retained displays.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's diagnostic evaluation, v2 adds useful evidence about training utility through disjoint training data, held-out gains, transfer tests, human-label checks, and detailed settings. However, new reporting problems weaken confidence: Figure 6 reverses the sampling instruction about contextual priors, and GPT-5's reported macro F1 of 78.61 disagrees with its class-wise average of approximately 78.14 in Tables 3 and 10. Claims about uncertainty reduction and human reasoning also exceed the direct measurements. These benefits and credibility problems leave the net quality direction uncertain.
